Introduction: Seeing Inside the Body

Imagine you are playing on a playground, you take a bad fall, and you suspect you’ve broken a bone. When you get to the hospital, what is the very first thing the doctor is going to do to figure out what is wrong? They aren’t going to just guess—they are going to take a special kind of photograph.

Medical imaging is not just like taking digital photos with our phones; it is an absolutely critical tool for diagnosing diseases and injuries. Without opening the body, how can we see what is happening inside? Today, we are going to explore the major medical imaging modalities. We will look at how they work, what kinds of diseases or injuries they are best suited to diagnose, and what their limitations are.

By the end of this lecture, you will understand the key components of these imaging scanners. More importantly, this will set the stage for our next lecture, where we will discuss how we can design nanomaterials—specifically contrast agents—to overcome the limitations of these machines and get even higher resolution images!

The Classic 2D View: X-Ray Imaging

X-ray imaging has a very long history. In fact, many of the imaging modalities we will discuss today were so revolutionary that they won Nobel Prizes. The very first Nobel Prize in Physics, in 1901, was awarded to Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen for his discovery of X-rays.

Take a look at the image on the right in the figure above. This is an original X-ray image of Röntgen’s wife’s hand, taken somewhat by accident! Even in this early, low-resolution image, we can clearly see the bones of her fingers. Notice the ring on her finger? It looks completely different from the bone.

Why does the ring look so dark and distinct? It all comes down to the mechanism of X-rays: different materials absorb X-rays differently based on their density and elemental composition. The metal ring absorbs X-rays much more strongly than the calcium and carbon-based tissues of our bones and flesh. This gives us a massive hint for our future nanoparticle designs: if we want to distinguish different tissues in the body, we could use metal-related nanomaterials to create that contrast!

X-rays are fantastic for spotting foreign objects or dense materials. A friend of mine recently had an accident where a small piece of stone shot into his hand while he was hitting stones together. An X-ray revealed the exact location of the stone instantly because its material properties were so different from human tissue. During the subsequent surgery to remove it, the doctors used a portable X-ray device to continuously monitor his hand in real-time.

Beyond broken bones and foreign objects, X-rays are widely used in other diagnostic areas.

Mammograms, which are X-ray examinations of the breast, are a crucial part of annual inspections for breast cancer. X-rays also played a massive role during the COVID-19 pandemic. If you look at a normal lung on an X-ray, it appears dark and clear because it is filled with air. But in a COVID-19 patient, we often see what is called a “white lung.” The high density of viral fluid and inflammation in the lung absorbs more X-rays, making it appear cloudy and white, allowing doctors to diagnose the severity of the infection.

The Disadvantages of X-Rays

While X-rays are incredibly useful, they have significant limitations. First, X-rays use ionizing radiation, which can damage DNA and potentially increase the risk of cancer. This is why X-ray rooms are heavily shielded. Have you ever noticed what metal is used to line the walls or the heavy aprons they put on you? It’s lead! Lead is incredibly dense and absorbs the harmful X-rays, protecting the rest of your body and the technicians.

Second, standard X-rays are only 2D images. If we spot a tumor on a 2D X-ray, we don’t know its exact depth. We have to take multiple images from different angles to estimate its 3D location.

Third, X-rays provide very poor details for soft tissues. We can see bones perfectly, but the intricate details of organs are mostly lost.

Finally, taking a clear X-ray requires the patient to stay completely still. For adults, this is easy. But for children? It’s a disaster! Because kids love to move around, hospitals sometimes have to use special, somewhat scary-looking clear containers to hold infants completely still while the image is taken. Motion is a terrible factor for X-ray clarity.

Adding Depth: Computed Tomography (CT)

How do we solve the 2D limitation of the X-ray? We use a computer to combine many X-rays into a 3D model! This brings us to Computed Tomography, or the CT scan. This invention was so groundbreaking that it won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1979, awarded to Allan M. Cormack and Godfrey N. Hounsfield. (In fact, the unit used to measure radiodensity in CT scans is called the Hounsfield unit).

Look at the comparison above. With a standard X-ray of the head, we only see the skull. But with a CT scan, we can see the bone and the soft tissue of the brain inside it! We can see fluids, different tissue densities, and distinct structures.

How does it work? A CT scanner is essentially an X-ray machine that rotates.

Inside the “donut” of the CT scanner, there is an X-ray producer on one side and an X-ray receptor (detector) on the exact opposite side. When a patient lies in the middle, this entire heavy apparatus rotates around them at extremely high speeds, taking thousands of X-ray slices from every possible angle. A computer then analyzes all these slices to reconstruct a full 3D image of the body.

Over the years, CT technology has evolved through several generations. Engineers optimized the distance between the producer and detector, widened the X-ray beam into a fan shape, and dramatically increased the rotation speed. Today, a modern CT scanner can scan an entire human body in just a few seconds!

The Magnetic Marvel: MRI

What if we want to see soft tissues with incredible detail, but we want to completely avoid the harmful ionizing radiation of X-rays and CT scans? Enter Magnetic Resonance Imaging, or MRI.

This technology is completely different from X-rays. It relies on the magnetic properties of the protons inside the water molecules in our bodies. The development of MRI was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2003 to Paul C. Lauterbur and Sir Peter Mansfield.

Think about the magnets you put on your refrigerator door. They align themselves to the metal. Similarly, the protons in our body can be forced to align in a specific direction if they are placed in a strong enough magnetic field.

To achieve this, an MRI machine uses a massive superconducting magnet. To keep it superconducting, the magnet is bathed in liquid helium. While the Earth’s magnetic field is tiny, a clinical MRI machine produces a magnetic field of 1.5 to 3 Tesla, and some advanced research machines (like the ones at Ohio State University) can go up to 8 Tesla! This intense magnetic field aligns the protons in your body.

The machine then uses a Radio Frequency (RF) coil to send a pulse of radio waves into the body. This pulse knocks the protons out of alignment. When the pulse is turned off, the protons realign with the magnetic field, and as they do, they release a signal. Different tissues (like fat vs. muscle vs. tumor) have different amounts of water and release signals at different rates. The MRI’s gradient coils help locate exactly where these signals are coming from, allowing a computer to build a stunningly detailed image of the soft tissues.

While MRI is incredible for soft tissue, it has notable disadvantages. First, it is a giant magnet! It is incredibly dangerous to bring any metal into the room. Patients with certain metal implants, pacemakers, or shrapnel cannot get an MRI. Second, it is very slow. While a CT scan takes seconds, an MRI of the brain might take nearly an hour, and a full-body scan could take half a day. The patient must lie perfectly still inside a tight, noisy tube for a long time, which can trigger severe claustrophobia.

Sound Waves: Ultrasound Imaging

If you want to check on the health of a developing baby in a pregnant woman, you cannot use X-rays or CT scans because the radiation is too dangerous. You also wouldn’t want to put a pregnant woman in a stressful, hour-long MRI tube. The perfect solution is Ultrasound imaging.

Ultrasound is incredibly safe because it uses high-frequency sound waves, not radiation. A handheld device called a transducer is placed on the skin. It emits sound waves into the body. When these sound waves hit a boundary between different tissues (like fluid and bone), they echo back. The transducer listens for these echoes, and a computer calculates how far away the boundary is based on how long the echo took to return, creating an image.

The main disadvantage of ultrasound is its limited resolution and detection scope. It is highly dependent on the operator, and it struggles to see through bone or air. If we are looking at a mass in the tissue, standard ultrasound often cannot tell us if it is a benign lump or a cancerous tumor. To solve this, researchers are developing specialized nanoparticles that can target specific tissues (like cancer) and enhance the ultrasound signal, which we will discuss in the next lecture!

Molecular Tracking: Nuclear Medical Imaging

All the modalities we’ve discussed so far are great at showing us the structure or anatomy of the body. But what if we want to see the function of the body at a molecular level? We use Nuclear Medical Imaging.

To do this, we must inject the patient with a special contrast agent called a radiopharmaceutical. This is a drug molecule that has been modified to include a radioactive isotope.

Because the drug is designed to participate in specific biological processes (like glucose metabolism), it will accumulate in specific areas of the body—for example, cancer cells consume a lot of glucose, so a radioactive glucose analog will gather inside tumors. As the isotope decays, it emits signals that we can detect.

There are two main types of nuclear imaging:

Positron Emission Tomography (PET)

In a PET scan, the injected isotope emits a positron (which is essentially a positively charged electron). When this positron travels a tiny distance and collides with a normal electron in the tissue, they annihilate each other! This annihilation produces two gamma rays that shoot out in exactly opposite directions.

The PET scanner is a ring of detectors. When it detects two gamma rays hitting opposite sides of the ring at the exact same time, it knows exactly where the annihilation happened along that line. This gives PET incredibly high sensitivity at the molecular level.

Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT)

SPECT is similar, but instead of emitting a positron, the injected isotope directly emits a single gamma ray.

We use a special gamma camera to detect these rays and build an image.

The major disadvantage of both PET and SPECT is that they require injecting radioactive materials into the patient, which carries risks. Furthermore, while they are highly sensitive to molecular activity, their spatial resolution is quite poor—they show glowing spots of activity, but you can’t see the surrounding anatomy (like bones or fat) to know exactly where that spot is. Because of this, PET and SPECT are almost always combined with a CT or MRI scan (e.g., a PET/CT scanner) so doctors can overlay the functional “glowing” image on top of the detailed anatomical structure.

Looking Ahead: The Role of Nanoparticles

We have covered a lot of ground today! We’ve looked at the major imaging modalities: MRI, CT, PET, SPECT, and Ultrasound.

Each of these machines has its own unique strengths and weaknesses. But what if we could make them all better? What if we could make tumors light up brighter on an MRI, or make specific blood vessels visible on an ultrasound?

This is where nanoscience comes in. Choosing the right imaging modality is only the first step. The next step is choosing the right contrast agent—the probe that we put into the body to enhance the image. As imaging technology has evolved over the last century, so too has the development of nanoparticles designed specifically to interact with these machines.

In our next lecture, we will dive into optical imaging and then explore exactly how we can fabricate and optimize nanoparticles to serve as the ultimate contrast agents for diagnosis!
